per_run.approach_summary: Profiled all 106 anonymized features, including cardinality, marginal target association, redundancy, and chronological versus stratified validation. Compared regularized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, random forest, several shallow LightGBM configurations, and CatBoost depths. Five-fold CV favored LightGBM, but the offline confirmation set showed better transfer from moderate-depth CatBoost; shallow LightGBM added complementary ranking information. The selected equal-weight percentile-rank blend of depth-4 CatBoost and 3-leaf LightGBM achieved confirmation AUC 0.8631, versus 0.8600 and 0.8575 individually. Final models were refit on all 5,000 labeled rows.

Explored all 106 anonymized features with stratified five-fold CV. Compared regularized logistic regression, LightGBM, ExtraTrees, and CatBoost, then tested tree complexity, importance-based feature pruning, and rank blends. Internal CV favored boosted-tree blends near 0.91 AUC, while confirmation feedback revealed distribution shift and favored shallower CatBoost. Across 20 permitted confirmation calls, the best AUC was 0.8709 for a rank blend of 65% depth-4 CatBoost, 25% depth-5 CatBoost on the 50 most important features, and 10% ExtraTrees. Final components were retrained on all 5,000 research rows.

Profiled all 106 anonymized features, missingness, cardinalities, univariate signal, row ordering, class imbalance, and temporal/block stability. Compared regularized LightGBM using all features and a signal-focused subset with CatBoost models of depths 4-8 and recent-window fits. Random/blocked LightGBM AUCs were 0.9148/0.8925, but its confirmation AUC was 0.8416. CatBoost generalized better: depth 4 scored 0.8631; depth 6 scored 0.8552, and a 70/30 depth-4/depth-6 seed ensemble scored 0.8639. I attacked that result as possible confirmation/regime overfit: contiguous-block validation was worse than random CV, training only the latest 3000/2000 rows scored 0.8411/0.8216, and importance-selected 30/60/80-feature ablations scored 0.8392/0.8478/0.8548. Thus there is genuine temporal drift and aggressive selection is brittle; no evidence supported a confirmation-only shortcut in the shallow all-feature ensemble. Deeper models and LightGBM blends also reduced confirmation AUC. Final approach is the same attacked 70/30 all-feature CatBoost depth-4/depth-6 ensemble, trained on all research rows.

Explored all 106 anonymized features, missingness/cardinality, univariate signal, shuffled and row-order-blocked validation. Compared histogram gradient boosting, Extra Trees, CatBoost, regularization/leaf-size variants, and probability/rank ensembles. Shuffled 5-fold AUC favored histogram boosting (~0.916), but confirmation reversed the ranking: histogram 0.8348, Extra Trees 0.8510, CatBoost 0.8507. An equal rank-average of Extra Trees (600 trees, leaf size 3, balanced fitting) and CatBoost (600 depth-6 iterations) scored best at 0.8567. I attacked this result as possible order/confirmation overfitting by measuring research-confirmation distribution shifts, checking chronological block validation, testing smoothing and alternative blends, and retraining on progressively newer subsets. The largest marginal KS shift was only ~0.08, while dropping older training rows degraded confirmation AUC from 0.8380 to 0.8095; the ensemble also combines models with distinct inductive biases. Thus the attack found drift/order sensitivity but no convincing confirmation-specific exploit, and I retained the conservative rank ensemble. The identical full-research-trained approach was applied to transfer and real_test.

Profiled all 106 anonymized features, including cardinality, missingness, univariate AUC/MI, feature correlations, subpopulation effects, chronological target variation, and distribution shift across research, confirmation, transfer, and real_test. The target was rare (3.7%). Sparse count features, especially x_012 and interacting fields among the early counts, plus irregular code fields, carried most signal; constant and weak fields added overfit risk. Compared logistic feature engineering, Extra Trees, Random Forest, histogram boosting, CatBoost, and multiple LightGBM capacities on five stratified and five blocked folds. The best random-fold models were near 0.91 AUC, while blocked validation was near 0.89-0.90. Offline confirmation feedback showed stronger drift/regularization effects: a regularized 7-leaf LightGBM trained on all research rows scored 0.8605, a selected-feature 15-leaf model trained on the most recent 4,000 rows scored 0.8560, and their 50/50 rank blend scored best at 0.8633. Broader all-model blends were worse. Final transfer and real_test predictions use that exact two-model rank blend, with both models refit as described.

Profiled all 106 features for missingness, cardinality, redundancy, univariate signal, duplicates, and population drift. Sparse count features and several strongly correlated derived feature blocks carried the main signal. Random forest, Extra Trees, LightGBM, CatBoost, histogram boosting, log-linear, quantile-bin, spline-additive, and feature-subset variants were compared. Tree models reached about 0.92 random-fold CV AUC but transferred poorly to the local confirmation population (roughly 0.821-0.842), revealing rare-cluster overfit. Log1p-transformed regularized logistic regression was much more stable: C=0.02 scored 0.8736 confirmation AUC, while a spline-additive model scored 0.8735. Rank blending these complementary additive models improved to 0.8793, and adding a conservative 10% Extra Trees contribution produced the best confirmation score, 0.8810. The fixed final blend (60% log-ridge, 30% spline-additive, 10% Extra Trees) was retrained on all 5,000 labeled rows; real_test was predicted in chunks.

Loaded all 106 anonymized features and profiled cardinality, missingness, marginal target signal, redundancy, exact duplicates, row-order behavior, and research/confirmation/transfer/real-test shifts. The labeled sample had 185 positives among 5,000 rows. I compared CatBoost, LightGBM, ExtraTrees, categorical CatBoost variants, full versus structural feature ablations, and probability/rank ensembles using stratified CV, consecutive blocked CV, and forward holdouts. Random-fold AUCs reached roughly 0.92, while blocked estimates were lower (about 0.87-0.89), so I did not trust random CV alone. Twenty local confirmation calls were used. Illustrative scores were 0.7030 for the strongest simple single-feature baseline, 0.8439 for all-feature LightGBM, 0.8169 for balanced all-feature CatBoost, 0.8637 for reduced unweighted CatBoost, and 0.8680 for the selected reduced rank ensemble. The final confirmation call tested exact-overlap correction and scored 0.8690. The selected model uses a 56-column structural view (features 0-19, 54-80, and 97-105), seed-averaged CatBoost depths 5 and 6, LightGBM, and ExtraTrees; their within-target ranks are blended 0.40/0.30/0.15/0.15. I attacked this result as possible campaign/duplicate and confirmation-block leakage. Exact research-confirmation matches were all negatives and correction changed AUC by only 0.001; five-fold blocked ensemble AUC was 0.8820 overall and 0.8818 after removing every exact train-validation overlap, so duplicates did not explain performance. Adversarial validation found only modest research-versus-confirmation/transfer separation (AUC 0.574/0.561), although real_test was more shifted (0.781). That real-test warning motivated retaining the reduced view, heterogeneous trees, and rank blending: these avoid noisy amount blocks, are insensitive to probability scale, and tree terminal splits limit extrapolation from outliers. The identical fitted pipeline and exact-match rule were applied to transfer and real_test.

Profiled all 106 anonymized features, missingness, cardinalities, shifts, correlations, duplicate vectors, and row-block prevalence. Compared LightGBM (7/15/31 leaves), random forests, ExtraTrees, and CatBoost with stratified and contiguous-block validation. Random 5-fold AUCs were about 0.905-0.911 for the strongest generic numeric models. Four high-cardinality identifier-like fields were then modeled categorically, with five pairwise identifier crosses, local unlabeled frequency encodings, and log/fractional amount features; depth-7 CatBoost reached 0.9232 stratified OOF AUC. Confirmation calls showed numeric baselines at 0.8261-0.8616 and the categorical depth-7 model at 0.8632. Exact feature-vector repeats were uniformly negative in research (26 duplicate groups, no conflicts), and ranking those repeats low raised confirmation AUC to the best 0.8662. I attacked this best approach for confirmation-specific category memorization and drift: categorical modeling still beat the numeric model on contiguous folds (0.8878 vs 0.8821) and whole-primary-identifier holdout (0.8540 vs 0.8334); large-test identifier overlap was comparable to confirmation (76.8%-98.8% depending on field). A five-seed ensemble fell to 0.8525 confirmation AUC, and recomputing frequencies over the much larger test population fell to 0.8594, so both were rejected as misleading extensions. Final predictions use the same attacked seed-52 depth-7 categorical model, local 8,000-row reference frequencies, and exact-negative-repeat rule for both targets.

DATA / STRUCTURE FINDINGS
106 anonymized features, 5000 labeled rows, 3.7% positive (185). Features fall into
interpretable blocks discovered from correlation + dominance structure:
 (a) x_000..x_013: event-type counts. These split into two near-collinear clusters:
     A = {000,002,004,005,006,009,010,013} (pairwise r 0.87-0.99) and
     B = {001,003,008,011,012} (pairwise r 0.49-0.97). Crucially, members of cluster A
     have OPPOSITE univariate target directions despite r~0.97 (x_000 AUC 0.619 vs
     x_013 AUC 0.262), so the signal lives in ratios/differences within A, not levels.
 (b) x_016-022, x_054-079, x_097-101: small ordinal counts.
 (c) x_023-041: near-constant flags (mostly 1; several are literally constant).
 (d) x_042-053 and x_081-096: two parallel monetary/amount blocks that pair up
     1:1 (042<->081, 043<->082, ... 053<->096, r 0.72-0.94) and are exactly equal in
     76-98% of rows -> they look like a (typical, extreme) pair of the same quantity;
     their ratio is a dispersion signal.
 (e) x_102-105: bounded numeric codes (x_102 in [1030,18366], x_103-105 offset by 100).

TWO-REGIME TARGET MECHANISM
sB = sum of cluster-B counts partitions the population almost perfectly into two
mechanisms: sB=0 -> 1.5% positive (3958 rows, 58 positives); sB>0 -> 12.2% (1042 rows,
127 positives), rising monotonically to ~100% for sB>20. Within the sB=0 subpopulation
the drivers are entirely different (low x_009/x_005/x_004, high x_015, high monetary
blocks x_092/x_083, small counts x_055/x_057/x_058/x_069) -- ~1/3 of all positives live
there and are invisible to the dominant B signal. I tested explicit regime-specific
models (separate learners per regime, rank-recombined): they were WORSE than one pooled
model (within-regime AUC 0.768 vs 0.824 for sB=0; 0.950 vs 0.961 for sB>0). The pooled
model already exploits the split; the regime structure is descriptive, not exploitable
by partitioning, because the small regime has too few positives to support its own model.

THE MAIN RESULT: CAPACITY, NOT FEATURES, IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT
Adversarial validation showed strong covariate shift between the labeled rows and the
large unlabeled target set: research-vs-real_test AUC 0.815 (0.505 on a research-vs-
research null, so the procedure is unbiased), and 0.885 restricted to research
positives, 0.815 restricted to research negatives -- i.e. the shift is NOT an artifact
of positive enrichment, it is a genuine covariate shift. research-vs-confirmation and
research-vs-transfer are ~0.60; confirmation-vs-real_test 0.795. Marginal KS distances
are small (max 0.14), so the shift is in the JOINT distribution, not the marginals.
Consequence: models that exploit high-order feature interactions overfit
research-specific joint structure and transfer badly. Measured directly:
    model                     research CV   confirmation AUC
    deep LGBM (31 leaves)        0.9244          0.8306
    7-model deep-tree ensemble   0.9266          0.8428
    depth-2 LGBM (+ratios)       0.8968          0.8630
    shallow+linear blend         ~0.90           0.8712 / 0.8682
The CV ranking is exactly INVERTED relative to the confirmation ranking. A -0.03 CV
sacrifice bought +0.04 transfer AUC.

FREE SHIFT-VALIDATION PROXY (the tool that made this tractable)
Confirmation has only ~55 positives, so its AUC SE is ~0.03 -- too noisy to tune on. I
built an offline substitute: fit a density-ratio model r(x)=p_real_test(x)/p_research(x)
by adversarial classification, sort the 5000 research rows by r(x), then train on the
low-r half and validate on the high-r half (and reverse). This synthesises the same kind
of shift internally. It predicted confirmation almost exactly, before I spent the calls:
    lgb1  shift-CV 0.8303 -> confirmation 0.8306
    d2F   shift-CV 0.8585 -> confirmation 0.8630
whereas plain random-split CV mispredicted both by +0.06 to +0.09. I then ran the whole
model sweep against shift-CV instead of CV. It shows a clean interior optimum in tree
depth: d1 0.863, d2 0.868, d3 0.865, d4 0.845, d6 0.846 (plain CV rises monotonically
0.877 -> 0.917 over the same range). Importance-weighted (density-ratio) training also
helped shift-CV (0.876) but I down-weighted that evidence as partly circular with the
weighting used to build the folds.
I also built an importance-weighted CV AUC estimator, but the effective sample size of
positives under the real_test weights collapsed to 34 of 185, making it too noisy to
select on -- I report it as a dead end.

FEATURE ENGINEERING
~90 engineered features: cluster A/B sums, B-fraction, nonzero counts, within-A
differences and ratios, per-pair monetary max/mean ratios and differences, block sums,
amount-per-count intensities, and rank/quantile transforms fitted on the real_test
marginals. On deep models these gave nothing (0.9107 vs 0.9113 -- the deep learner
already recovers them). On depth-1/2 models they are worth +0.01 (d1: 0.876 -> 0.887),
which is the expected result: explicit ratios substitute for the interaction capacity
the constrained model no longer has. This is why the final blend uses them.

FINAL MODEL
Rank-average of 16 models in three groups, weights 0.45 / 0.30 / 0.25:
 T (0.45) 8 shallow gradient-boosted models: depth 1/2/3 over raw, raw+engineered, and
   real_test-quantile views, plus a monotone-constrained depth-2 (constraints signed by
   univariate direction) and two extra_trees-mode variants.
 F (0.30) 6 random forests / extremely randomized forests at two regularisation levels
   (min_samples_leaf 2 and 8) over raw+engineered and quantile views.
 L (0.25) 2 linear models: L2 logistic on cubic-spline bases of quantile-transformed
   features, and on quantile + log-engineered features.
Each fit on all 5000 research rows (3 seeds for boosted models). The linear component is
individually the weakest on CV (0.88) but degrades least under shift and is the least
correlated member (Spearman ~0.5 vs the tree consensus); removing it costs ~0.002-0.005
confirmation AUC. Group weights, rather than a greedy per-model search, because greedy
selection on 4 shift folds / 55 confirmation positives is pure noise-fitting: every
blend I tested in this family landed in 0.865-0.871.

CONFIRMATION LOOP (15 calls)
0.8428 deep 4-model ensemble -> 0.8306 single deep LGBM -> 0.8449 linear alone (the
result that flagged complexity as the problem) -> 0.8453 all-8 blend -> 0.8630 depth-2
-> 0.8697 shallow+linear -> 0.8594 50/50 deep+shallow -> 0.8689 shallow+forests ->
0.8712 shallow+forests+linear -> 0.866/0.8653/0.8649 (16-model variants) -> 0.8682 final
group blend, re-verified at 0.8682 through the exact artifact-writing code path.
I stopped tuning once every candidate sat inside 0.865-0.871: that spread is one
confirmation-set standard error, and further selection would be fitting 55 positives.

CAVEAT
real_test is more shifted from research than confirmation is (adversarial 0.815 vs 0.60),
so I expect its AUC to sit below the 0.868 confirmation number. That is precisely why the
final model is deliberately capacity-limited rather than CV-optimal.

DATA / STRUCTURE FINDINGS (all derived from research.json alone plus the unlabeled pools)

Shape: 5,000 labeled rows, 106 anonymized features, target prevalence 3.70% (185 positives).
1,500 confirmation rows, 1,500 transfer rows, 506,691 real_test rows.

I first mapped the feature space rather than modeling it. Comparing exact zero-patterns
across columns recovered the schema:
  * 27 exact (count, amount) pairs -- e.g. x_016<->x_047, x_043<->x_098, x_054<->x_081,
    x_069<->x_092 -- where a column is nonzero iff its partner is. These form four
    count blocks (x_016-022, x_097-101, x_054-064, x_068-079) with matching amount
    blocks (x_047-053, x_042-046, x_081-090, x_089-096).
  * A near-degenerate "capacity/flag" block (x_023-041, x_065-067, x_080), almost all
    constant at 1.
  * Four encoded categoricals offset by +100: x_102 (1,436 levels), x_103 (359),
    x_104 (29, 87% concentrated on 150), x_105 (40).
  * A 15-column "head" block x_000..x_014 of nested counts. Dominance checks showed
    strict containment: x_004>=x_005, x_000>=x_005, x_002>=x_003, x_006>=x_011,
    x_008>=x_012, x_010>=x_011 in 100% of rows -- i.e. totals and sub-type counts of
    the same activity.
  * Within the head block, two clusters: a "bulk volume" cluster (x_000,002,004,005,
    006,009,010,013; pairwise r = 0.87-0.99) and a "special-event" cluster
    (x_001,003,008,011,012; r = 0.5-0.97). The clusters are nearly orthogonal to each
    other (r ~ 0.0-0.2).

Two structural facts about the target:
  * A hard regime gate. x_078>0 (equivalently the x_077/x_078/x_079 triple) implies
    x_009=0 AND x_013=0 in every row, with no exceptions; and x_078>0 is a strict
    subset of "special cluster nonzero" (965 of the 1,042 rows with special counts;
    the 77 rows with special counts but x_078=0 contain zero positives). Inside the
    gate the positive rate is 13.2% (127/965); outside it is 1.4% (58/4,035).
  * THE KEY FINDING: levels are far less informative than RATIOS within the head
    block. The best single raw feature is x_012 (AUC 0.789). The single ratio
    x_000/x_005 reaches AUC 0.834 overall and 0.867 inside the gate -- despite
    x_000 and x_005 being 0.97-correlated. The same effect flips signs across the
    gate: x_000 has AUC 0.809 inside the gate but 0.438 outside; x_004/x_005/x_009/
    x_013 are negative predictors overall (AUC 0.26-0.33), and P(y|x_004=0)=0.201 vs
    P(y|x_004>0)=0.027. In words: risk is about the MIX of activity types, not the
    amount of activity; a profile whose totals are not backed by the bulk sub-type
    is the high-risk profile. Trees cannot express a ratio of two features directly,
    which is why this structure is invisible to a plain gradient-boosted model on the
    raw columns.

WHAT I BUILT

Feature set: the 106 raw columns plus all 105 pairwise log-ratios log1p(x_i)-log1p(x_j)
among x_000..x_014 (211 features). This was the single largest gain of the whole run:
repeated-stratified 5-fold CV rose from 0.9141 to 0.9222 (better in every one of 6
repeats), and the local confirmation proxy rose 0.8349 -> 0.8513.

Things I tested that did NOT help, and I dropped: count/amount averages, block totals
and shares, ratio expansions beyond the head block (block sums: 0.9118; a top-25
feature ratio basis: 0.9191; head+count-block basis: 0.9167 -- all worse than head-only
0.9219-0.9233); out-of-fold target encoding of x_102/x_103/x_105 (0.8986, badly worse);
LightGBM native categorical handling (0.9140); frequency encoding of the categoricals
from the 506k unlabeled pool (+0.001, noise); pool-computed group-normalised z-scores
of head features within x_103/x_105 groups (0.9194-0.9205, worse); a duplicate-
multiplicity feature from the pooled unlabeled rows (univariate AUC 0.508, useless --
though all 26 exact-duplicate groups inside research are all-negative, low-activity
profiles). Dropping the high-cardinality x_015/x_102/x_103 cost 0.010; replacing them
with 20-bin quantile versions was exactly neutral, which showed their signal is real
and not value-level memorisation.

Model: LightGBM (num_leaves 20, min_child_samples 60, colsample 1.0, subsample 0.8,
600 trees @ lr 0.02, reg_lambda 5, scale_pos_weight 26), averaged over 10 seeds,
rank-blended 3:1 with a class-balanced ExtraTrees (1500 trees, min_samples_leaf 2,
max_features 0.3) on the same 211 features. scale_pos_weight was worth ~+0.003 CV
(0.9233 -> 0.9266, monotone in the weight up to ~26-50). Final 8-repeat 5-fold CV:
LightGBM alone 0.9290 +- 0.0081, the 3:1 blend 0.9293 +- 0.0083. CatBoost (0.9169)
and a second LightGBM parameterisation (0.9263) were tried and added nothing.

VALIDATION AND WHAT THE CONFIRMATION SCORES TOLD ME

Eight scorer calls: 0.8349 (raw LightGBM), 0.8513 (add head log-ratios), 0.8383
(CV-tuned LightGBM alone), 0.8524 (3xLGB + 1xET), 0.8487, 0.8526, 0.8494, 0.8484
(other blend weightings).

Two lessons. First, the ratio features replicated out of sample (+0.016). Second, the
CV-optimal SINGLE model was the worst submission of the eight (0.8383) while every
blend landed at 0.848-0.853: past the feature-set gain, further single-model tuning
was fitting CV noise, and averaging over model families recovered it. I therefore
selected the 3:1 LightGBM/ExtraTrees blend, which is jointly top on CV (0.9293) and
top-tier on the proxy (0.8524), rather than the CV-best single model.

I also spent effort on the ~0.08 gap between CV (0.929) and the proxy (0.852), because
it was too large to accept as noise (bootstrapping 1,500-row subsamples of my OOF gives
sd 0.021, so 0.852 is ~3.5 sigma low). Three checks:
  * Group structure. Grouped CV by x_102 collapses to 0.830 and by x_103 to 0.846, so
    those columns are area/entity-like and random folds exploit within-group label
    correlation. But this is NOT a validation artifact: 81.2% of validation rows in a
    random fold have their x_102 level present in the training fold, versus 81.3% for
    confirmation, 80.0% for transfer and 76.8% for real_test. Random K-fold reproduces
    the real overlap regime almost exactly, so grouped CV is too pessimistic here.
  * Ordering. Row order carries mild drift (Spearman rho ~ -0.07, p ~ 1e-7, for the
    special-cluster counts; adversarial AUC between the first and second half of
    research is 0.618, the same 0.61 measured research-vs-confirmation and
    research-vs-transfer). But a strict forward split (train rows 0-3499, validate
    3500-4999) scored 0.9159, identical to the mean of random 3500/1500 splits
    (0.9161 +- 0.034). So drift is real but not the explanation.
  * Cohort size. Leave-one-block-out AUCs on contiguous 1,000-row blocks are 0.857,
    0.838, 0.931, 0.953, 0.843 (mean ~0.88) while the pooled OOF AUC over all blocks
    is 0.927. The gap is the standard pooled-vs-within-cohort AUC difference: a single
    1,500-row cohort like confirmation measures within-cohort discrimination (~0.88
    +- 0.03), and 0.852 sits inside that. So the two numbers are consistent; they
    simply measure different things. I kept random-fold CV for model ranking and used
    the proxy only to detect over-tuning, which is exactly what it caught.

REAL_TEST AND COVARIATE SHIFT

real_test is a separate, differently composed pool, not a larger draw of the same
sample. The special-cluster prevalence is materially higher there: P(x_003>0) is 0.276
vs 0.131 in research (a 29-sigma difference at these sample sizes), P(x_001>0) 0.268 vs
0.183, P(x_012>0) 0.272 vs 0.195, while x_011 is unshifted at 0.135 vs 0.130. The
x_105 level 202 (6.8% of research rows) is entirely absent from real_test, and
real_test carries missing values in x_004/x_014/x_054-x_096 that never occur in
research. Adversarial validation research-vs-real_test is 0.882 versus 0.61 for
research-vs-confirmation. Since the special cluster is the strongest positive
predictor, the implied real_test base rate is somewhat higher than 3.7% (~4.6% under a
stable conditional).

This shift is the reason I chose the log-ratio representation and a blend rather than
the CV-best single model: log-ratios are scale-free, so they extrapolate into
real_test's much longer tails (x_000 reaches 1,501 there vs 341 in research) instead of
saturating at the last training split. The check bears this out -- the top-1% ranked
real_test rows have the same qualitative profile as the top-1% OOF research rows
(median log(x_000/x_005) 2.40 vs 2.27; the research top 1% is 100% positive).

Final predictions are rank-averages within each target set: 3x the 10-seed LightGBM
plus 1x ExtraTrees, both retrained on all 5,000 research rows. transfer_predictions
covers all 1,500 transfer rows; final_predictions.csv covers all 506,691 real_test rows.

STRUCTURE FOUND
The four highest-numbered columns are not numeric measurements at all: x_102 (13,244
levels), x_103 (497), x_104 (115) and x_105 (102) are label-encoded categoricals whose codes
are dense integer runs starting at exactly 1001 / 100 / 100 / 100, with strongly skewed level
frequencies. Cross-tabulating them shows a strict nesting: every x_102 code maps to exactly
one x_103 code (99.9%) and one x_104 code (100.0%), and x_103 maps to one x_104 (96.6%).
So x_102 is an entity id inside a two-level taxonomy, and rows sharing x_102 are repeated
observations of one entity. 83% of research rows sit in an entity with more than one row;
81% of confirmation, 80% of transfer and 77% of real_test rows belong to an entity that also
appears in research. Within research, entities containing a positive are only ~11% positive,
so entity identity multiplies the prior ~3x but does not determine the label.
Hierarchical correlation clustering of the other 102 columns recovers repeating
(count-block, magnitude-block) triples -- e.g. (x_017,x_018,x_019) with (x_048,x_049,x_050),
(x_020,x_021,x_022) with (x_051,x_052,x_053), (x_068..x_070) with (x_091..x_093) -- which
I turned into per-cluster totals and per-item ratios. One cluster
(x_001,x_008,x_012,x_077,x_078,x_079) carries most of the univariate signal: those columns
are nonzero for 21% of rows but for 69% of positives (individual AUCs 0.75-0.79).

WHAT I BUILT
Because the labelled sample is tiny (5000 rows, 185 positives) but the unlabelled corpus is
huge (506,691 real_test rows, median 752 rows per entity), the entity structure lets me
estimate a low-variance profile for each entity from unlabelled data: the mean and sd of 24
informative columns over all real_test rows of that entity, the row's deviation from that
mean, and the same means at the x_103 and x_104 levels. Profiles are computed from real_test
only and leave-one-out, so no row ever contributes to its own profile. Final model: an
equal-weight rank blend of two ensembles, each {LightGBM, LightGBM-GOSS, RandomForest} x 5
seeds trained on all 5000 research rows -- (A) with the profile block, (B) without it.

VALIDATION AND WHAT THE CONFIRMATION SCORES SAID
Two CV schemes: plain stratified 5-fold, and 5-fold grouped by x_102 (novel entities). The
random scheme is deployment-matched on entity overlap -- it leaves 81.1% of validation rows
in an entity seen in training, against the 81.3% research->confirmation overlap I measured.
Raw 106 features: 0.919 random / 0.812 group. Adding cluster engineering + entity profiles:
0.9395 random / 0.8869 group (5 seeds, ensembled).
Seven scorer calls: raw LightGBM 0.8335; engineered LightGBM 0.8378; earlier-generation
ensemble 0.8386; RandomForest alone 0.8298; final profile ensemble 0.8333; the same ensemble
with the profile block removed 0.8405; the 50/50 blend 0.8421. Every model, including the
unengineered baseline, sits ~0.09 below its research CV, so the level offset is a property of
the confirmation sample rather than of anything I added; and the spread across seven very
different models is only 0.012, so this proxy resolves almost nothing about model choice.
Model *ranking* on confirmation tracked random CV, not group CV (RandomForest was best under
group CV but worst on confirmation), which is why I kept random CV as the primary metric.

ATTACKING MY OWN BEST APPROACH
1. Arbitrary code order. If the model were riding the meaningless numeric ordering of the ID
   codes it would be fragile. Consistently relabelling all four ID columns with a random
   bijection across every dataset left CV unchanged (0.9290 -> 0.9295 / 0.9284), and deleting
   the raw ID columns outright also changed nothing (0.9299). They are now dropped entirely.
2. Coincidental overlap. 31 research rows are exact duplicates of confirmation rows (all
   negative, 2% of confirmation); CV computed with those rows excluded is *higher* (0.9329 vs
   0.9290), so duplicate memorisation is not carrying the score.
3. Self-contribution in the transductive profiles. Rebuilding every profile from real_test
   alone -- disjoint from research/confirmation/transfer, so no evaluated row can contribute
   to its own profile -- did not shrink the gain, it grew it (0.9299/0.8532 -> 0.9340/0.8749).
   That is now the shipped construction.
4. Negative control. Keeping the whole profile machinery but attaching each row to a RANDOM
   entity collapsed random CV to 0.886-0.895, i.e. below the 0.9164 no-profile baseline. The
   gain is genuinely carried by the entity linkage, not by the extra columns.
5. Entity-mean smoothing. Averaging predictions over each entity's unlabelled rows -- the
   obvious exploit if labels were constant per entity -- destroys performance (0.80 vs 0.93
   alone; blending is monotonically harmful). Correctly so: positives are only 11% of the rows
   inside positive entities. Rejected.
6. THE ATTACK THAT LANDED. Holding everything else fixed, the profile block is worth +0.021
   on research OOF (0.9395 vs 0.9187) but -0.007 on the confirmation region (0.8333 vs
   0.8405). Bootstrapping paired 1500-row subsets of the research OOF puts the sd of that
   paired difference at 0.0114, so a -0.007 outcome has probability ~0.004 under my CV
   estimate. Too unlikely to wave away as noise. Decomposing the block under progressively
   coarser grouped CV shows why it is suspect: under CV grouped by x_104 (entire coarse
   branches held out) the profiles turn actively harmful (0.7796 without vs 0.7658 with),
   i.e. part of what they supply is coarse-group identity that only pays off when the same
   branches appear in train and test. That is the deployment regime here (98.8% of real_test
   rows sit in an x_104 branch seen in research), but it is a fragile thing to lean on.
   Rather than finalise the CV-optimal model, I ship the equal-weight blend of the profile
   and no-profile ensembles. The two are only 0.68 rank-correlated. It costs 0.007 random CV
   and 0.016 group CV against the CV-optimal weight, and it was the best of all seven
   submissions on the held-out confirmation region (0.8421, above both components). w=0.5 was
   fixed a priori as an equal hedge between two defensible families, not tuned on the proxy.

HONEST BOTTOM LINE
Expected AUC on real_test is most likely in the 0.84-0.93 band. Research CV for the shipped
blend is 0.9326 random / 0.8707 grouped-by-entity; the confirmation region reads 0.8421.
real_test has lower entity overlap with research (77% vs 81%), a far broader entity universe
(13,244 vs 1,436 codes), noticeably heavier count features and ~50x more missing values than
research, so I expect it to land nearer the grouped-CV end than the random-CV end.
The same final blend was applied unchanged to transfer.json and real_test.csv.

DATA / STRUCTURE. 5000 labelled rows, 106 anonymised features, 3.7% positive (185 positives); 1500 confirmation, 1500 transfer, 506,691 real_test rows. Four columns are not really numeric: x_102 behaves as an entity/group id (1,436 levels in research, 13,244 in real_test, largest group = 6% of research rows), x_103 as a 359-level code, and x_104 (29 levels, 87% = "150") / x_105 (40 levels) as low-cardinality risk strata. The remaining 102 columns are counts and float aggregates. Eight of them (x_001/003/008/011/012/077/078/079) form one tight latent construct (pairwise Spearman 0.64-1.00) and are the strongest univariate predictors (best single-feature AUC 0.789).

VALIDATION DESIGN -- the decision that mattered most. Plain StratifiedKFold on the research rows reports AUC 0.91-0.92; StratifiedGroupKFold on x_102 reports 0.83-0.89. My first confirmation submission (a LightGBM tuned under random CV) scored 0.8183, i.e. the grouped number, not the random one. I therefore discarded random CV entirely and selected on grouped CV, cross-checked with an importance-weighted variant: I fit an out-of-fold adversarial classifier research-vs-target, converted its scores to a density ratio, and computed a weighted Mann-Whitney AUC on the grouped OOF predictions -- giving performance estimates under the confirmation and real_test covariate distributions using research labels (positive effective sample size 117 and 55 respectively).

MODEL CLASS BEAT TUNING. On identical features, an ExtraTreesClassifier (1000 trees, min_samples_leaf 5, max_features 1.0) on log1p-transformed numerics plus one-hot dummies for x_104/x_105 -- x_102 and x_103 dropped -- reached grouped CV 0.883, versus 0.850 for a 96-point-grid-tuned LightGBM, 0.855 HistGB, 0.846 CatBoost, 0.874 RF, 0.837 L2-logistic. Confirmation agreed: ET 0.8330 vs LightGBM 0.8183. Encoding mattered as much as the learner: removing the x_104/x_105 dummies costs 0.034 grouped AUC, and adding x_103 as one-hot costs 0.023 (its cardinality lets the model memorise groups). Engineered density/ratio features, MLP, kNN, LightGBM's extra_trees mode, class weighting, bootstrap ET and stratum-specific models all failed to improve on it.

FINAL MODEL. Rank-average of two blocks: an ET block (ET on log1p features, ET on rank-transformed features, ET plus engineered ratios, bootstrap ET) at weight 0.55, and a deliberately diverse block (LightGBM, CatBoost, HistGB, RandomForest, L2-logistic) at weight 0.45; 3 seeds each, trained on all 5000 research rows. Confirmation ledger (10 calls): LGBM baseline 0.8183; ET 0.8330; ET block 0.8364; ET block + light diversity 0.8463; ET + group target encoding 0.8027; diverse block alone 0.8541; 50/50 0.8505; final 55/45 0.8500; x_104xx_105 lookup baseline 0.7513; production-code-path replication of the final blend 0.8500 (a check that the chunked real_test code reproduces the validated number exactly -- it did).

WHY 55/45 AND NOT THE CONFIRMATION OPTIMUM. Grouped CV and both importance-weighted variants rank the ET block ABOVE the diverse block by 0.02-0.03; confirmation ranks it BELOW by 0.018. By subsampling 1500 rows from the research OOF predictions, the paired-AUC sampling SD at this size (55 positives) is 0.014, so the disagreement is ~2.5 SD -- real, but not decisive, and grouped CV is upward-biased for ET because I selected ET's configuration on it. I did not chase the confirmation optimum (which would be the diverse block alone, 0.8541); the 55/45 blend is within 0.005 of the best value under every metric I have, including the real_test-weighted estimate, which peaks at a nonzero diverse weight (0.9012 at w=0.40, 0.9001 at w=0).

ATTACK ON MY OWN BEST APPROACH. I ran four attacks aimed at showing the confirmation score is misleading.
(1) Fold artifact / group memorisation -- SUCCEEDED, and changed the model. Adding a smoothed out-of-fold target encoding of x_102/x_103 raised random-CV AUC from 0.911 to 0.920, but LOWERED confirmation from 0.8330 to 0.8027. Group-identity signal here is a fold artifact, not transferable structure, even though 81% of confirmation rows and 77% of real_test rows share an x_102 value with some research row. The final model contains no target encoding and no x_102/x_103.
(2) Coincidental overlap with research rows -- FAILED to overturn. 30 of 1500 confirmation rows (and 28 of 1500 transfer rows) are exact feature duplicates of a research row. Every one of those twins is a negative, 90% are near-empty rows, and the model ranks them at mean percentile 0.164. They are trivially-easy negatives that any model would rank low from the features alone, not memorisation; their contribution is bounded around 0.01 AUC.
(3) Spurious dominant feature -- FAILED to overturn. Deleting all eight of the most univariately predictive features costs nothing: grouped 0.8863 -> 0.8855, and the confirmation-weighted estimate actually improves, 0.8721 -> 0.8750. 58 of 115 model columns carry positive permutation importance and the single most important one (x_092) has a univariate AUC of only 0.595, so the model is running on broad multivariate structure, not one leak-shaped column. Conversely, those eight features plus x_104/x_105 alone reach only 0.754.
(4) "It is really just a lookup table" -- PARTLY SUCCEEDED, and it recalibrated the claim rather than the model. A predictor built solely from the smoothed target rate of the x_104 x x_105 cross -- 27 distinct values, zero row-level information -- scores 0.7513 on confirmation. So roughly three quarters of the headline number is two categorical risk strata. The remaining ~0.10 is genuine row-level discrimination, and the within-stratum grouped OOF AUCs confirm it is real but very uneven: 0.972 inside x_104=185 (16.9% positive, 11% of rows) versus 0.797 inside x_104=150 (2.1% positive, 87% of rows). Fitting separate models per stratum did not help (global model within x_104=185: 0.973 vs stratum-local 0.966), so the single global ET is already learning the stratum-conditional structure rather than just the base rates.

DISTRIBUTION SHIFT TO real_test. Adversarial validation with a null calibrated on a random 3500/1500 split of research (0.504): research vs confirmation 0.610, research vs transfer 0.627, research vs real_test 0.824. real_test is materially further from the training distribution than either held-out set, which is why I kept the diverse block rather than shipping the strongest single grouped-CV model. Sanity checks on the shipped real_test predictions: x_104=185 rows average rank 0.657 vs 0.479 for x_104=150, and 36% of the predicted top decile is x_104=185 (10.6% of rows), a 3.4x enrichment consistent with the research-set relationship.

The identical blend, trained on all 5000 research rows, produced both transfer_predictions and final_predictions.csv (all 506,691 rows).
